He had a history of hypothyroidism and dyslipidemia, for which he took levothyroxine and rosuvastatin. He reported no changes in visual acuity or color vision; no ocular pain, erythema, or abnormal discharge; and no headaches, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria, weakness, numbness, or ataxia. He did not have any constitutional or systemic symptoms. Physical examination showed an isolated limitation of right eye abduction. The remainder of the examination, including visual acuity, pupillary reaction, visual fields, and fundoscopy, was unremarkable. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the head showed abnormal thickening and T2 hyperintensity of the right lateral rectus muscle with T1-weighted gadolinium enhancement (Figure 1). case_info.explanation: This case illustrates the diagnostic considerations of a patient with enlarged extraocular muscles. Ocular lymphoma can cause weakness of the enlarged extraocular muscles, whereas metastatic deposits result in a restrictive pattern.1Features of malignancy include the presence of a focal mass, irregular edges, or nodularity within the muscle.2Although single muscle involvement is often seen in idiopathic inflammatory orbital myositis, the lack of pain argues against the diagnosis. IgG4-related disease is well documented to involve extraocular muscles, commonly producing a restrictive pattern.4IgG4-related disease can affect both the muscle belly and its tendinous attachment, whereas thyroid orbitopathy typically spares the tendon.2Notably, the lateral rectus is disproportionately involved in patients with singular or multiple muscle involvement.2Biopsy of the affected lateral rectus muscle revealed a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease, ruling out other such considerations as metastatic disease, giant cell myositis, sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and amyloidosis (Figure 2). IgG4-related disease is an insidious, progressive, multisystem fibroinflammatory disease that can affect hepatobiliary ducts, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes, salivary glands, retroperitoneum, pancreas, and lymph nodes, among other areas.5Its prevalence is estimated at 0.28 to 1.08 per 100 000 individuals,5with a mean age at diagnosis in the late 50s.6Although IgG4-related disease is slightly more prevalent in men (1:0.64-0.77), IgG4-related orbital disease (IgG4-ROD) affects men and women equally.6IgG4-ROD most commonly affects the lacrimal gland but can also affect extraocular muscles, orbit, adnexal soft tissue, and the cavernous sinus.6Other neurological involvement includes hypertrophic pachymeningitis, hypophysitis, peripheral neuropathy, and parenchymal disease.6 Although not well understood, the pathogenesis of IgG4-related disease involves complex immunogenic interactions between B cells and CD4+T lymphocytes within the affected organ, leading to release of local cytokines that produce an irregular, whorled pattern of fibrosis (“storiform fibrosis”) at the site of disease.5,6Within a germinal center of a lymph node or other lymphoid tissue, B cells also undergo preferential production of IgG4, and T helper cells facilitate class switching to IgG4.5,6In a healthy adult, IgG4 comprises less than 5% of the body’s immunoglobulins.7Elevated IgG4 levels above 135 mg/L support a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease, but this may be normal in 30% of patients.7 Most patients with IgG4-ROD present with bilateral eyelid swelling and proptosis; however, diplopia is the presenting feature in one-third of patients.6IgG4-ROD results in a lesser degree of restrictive strabismus and diplopia than thyroid orbitopathy, despite having greater extraocular enlargement.4MRI may demonstrate a well-defined tumorlike mass within the structures of the orbit and/or abnormal thickening of extraocular muscles. The regions of abnormality are isointense on T1, have variable patterns of T2 signal change, and homogenously enhance on postgadolinium images.8Enlargement of the infraorbital nerve on MRI is a specific sign for IgG4-ROD but lacks sensitivity.9Involvement of the infraorbital nerve is minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic, as infiltration is typically limited to the epineurium.4In the absence of reliable serological and radiographical markers, the diagnosis of IgG4-ROD hinges on histopathological confirmation of lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with an increased ratio of IgG4-positive to IgG-positive plasmacytes equal to or greater than 40%, or more than 50 IgG4-positive cells per high-power field.10The classic findings of storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis in IgG4-related disease are less frequently seen in IgG4-ROD compared with other sites of disease.10 Early recognition and treatment can prevent long-term complications and death in patients with IgG4-related disease. On confirmation of IgG4-ROD, treatment with high-dose corticosteroids and rituximab should be initiated. Although systemic IgG4-related disease may be treated with corticosteroid monotherapy, combination therapy of corticosteroids and rituximab is preferred in patients with severe disease, neurological involvement, and high IgG4 levels.6

case_info.explanation: This case illustrates the diagnostic considerations of a patient with enlarged extraocular muscles. Although this most commonly occurs in thyroid eye disease, the patient was euthyroid and did not have the typical restrictive pattern of ocular dysmotility, whereby duction in the opposite direction of the enlarged muscle is impaired.1Thyroid orbitopathy classically affects a combination of the inferior rectus, medial rectus, and/or levator palpebrae superioris.2Isolated involvement of the lateral rectus, superior rectus, or oblique muscles is virtually absent in thyroid disease.2Ocular lymphoma involving the extraocular muscles is rare, with 1 review identifying 46 cases in the literature3; it more commonly affects the lacrimal glands or the intraconal or extraconal orbital compartment. Ocular lymphoma can cause weakness of the enlarged extraocular muscles, whereas metastatic deposits result in a restrictive pattern.1Features of malignancy include the presence of a focal mass, irregular edges, or nodularity within the muscle.2Although single muscle involvement is often seen in idiopathic inflammatory orbital myositis, the lack of pain argues against the diagnosis. IgG4-related disease is well documented to involve extraocular muscles, commonly producing a restrictive pattern.4IgG4-related disease can affect both the muscle belly and its tendinous attachment, whereas thyroid orbitopathy typically spares the tendon.2Notably, the lateral rectus is disproportionately involved in patients with singular or multiple muscle involvement.2Biopsy of the affected lateral rectus muscle revealed a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease, ruling out other such considerations as metastatic disease, giant cell myositis, sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and amyloidosis (Figure 2). IgG4-related disease is an insidious, progressive, multisystem fibroinflammatory disease that can affect hepatobiliary ducts, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes, salivary glands, retroperitoneum, pancreas, and lymph nodes, among other areas.5Its prevalence is estimated at 0.28 to 1.08 per 100 000 individuals,5with a mean age at diagnosis in the late 50s.6Although IgG4-related disease is slightly more prevalent in men (1:0.64-0.77), IgG4-related orbital disease (IgG4-ROD) affects men and women equally.6IgG4-ROD most commonly affects the lacrimal gland but can also affect extraocular muscles, orbit, adnexal soft tissue, and the cavernous sinus.6Other neurological involvement includes hypertrophic pachymeningitis, hypophysitis, peripheral neuropathy, and parenchymal disease.6 Although not well understood, the pathogenesis of IgG4-related disease involves complex immunogenic interactions between B cells and CD4+T lymphocytes within the affected organ, leading to release of local cytokines that produce an irregular, whorled pattern of fibrosis (“storiform fibrosis”) at the site of disease.5,6Within a germinal center of a lymph node or other lymphoid tissue, B cells also undergo preferential production of IgG4, and T helper cells facilitate class switching to IgG4.5,6In a healthy adult, IgG4 comprises less than 5% of the body’s immunoglobulins.7Elevated IgG4 levels above 135 mg/L support a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease, but this may be normal in 30% of patients.7 Most patients with IgG4-ROD present with bilateral eyelid swelling and proptosis; however, diplopia is the presenting feature in one-third of patients.6IgG4-ROD results in a lesser degree of restrictive strabismus and diplopia than thyroid orbitopathy, despite having greater extraocular enlargement.4MRI may demonstrate a well-defined tumorlike mass within the structures of the orbit and/or abnormal thickening of extraocular muscles. The regions of abnormality are isointense on T1, have variable patterns of T2 signal change, and homogenously enhance on postgadolinium images.8Enlargement of the infraorbital nerve on MRI is a specific sign for IgG4-ROD but lacks sensitivity.9Involvement of the infraorbital nerve is minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic, as infiltration is typically limited to the epineurium.4In the absence of reliable serological and radiographical markers, the diagnosis of IgG4-ROD hinges on histopathological confirmation of lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with an increased ratio of IgG4-positive to IgG-positive plasmacytes equal to or greater than 40%, or more than 50 IgG4-positive cells per high-power field.10The classic findings of storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis in IgG4-related disease are less frequently seen in IgG4-ROD compared with other sites of disease.10 Early recognition and treatment can prevent long-term complications and death in patients with IgG4-related disease. On confirmation of IgG4-ROD, treatment with high-dose corticosteroids and rituximab should be initiated. Although systemic IgG4-related disease may be treated with corticosteroid monotherapy, combination therapy of corticosteroids and rituximab is preferred in patients with severe disease, neurological involvement, and high IgG4 levels.6

case_info.caption: Magnetic resonance image of the head demonstrating enlargement of the right lateral rectus muscle with homogenous gadolinium enhancement (arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: This case illustrates the diagnostic considerations of a patient with enlarged extraocular muscles. Although this most commonly occurs in thyroid eye disease, the patient was euthyroid and did not have the typical restrictive pattern of ocular dysmotility, whereby duction in the opposite direction of the enlarged muscle is impaired.1Thyroid orbitopathy classically affects a combination of the inferior rectus, medial rectus, and/or levator palpebrae superioris.2Isolated involvement of the lateral rectus, superior rectus, or oblique muscles is virtually absent in thyroid disease.2Ocular lymphoma involving the extraocular muscles is rare, with 1 review identifying 46 cases in the literature3; it more commonly affects the lacrimal glands or the intraconal or extraconal orbital compartment. Ocular lymphoma can cause weakness of the enlarged extraocular muscles, whereas metastatic deposits result in a restrictive pattern.1Features of malignancy include the presence of a focal mass, irregular edges, or nodularity within the muscle.2Although single muscle involvement is often seen in idiopathic inflammatory orbital myositis, the lack of pain argues against the diagnosis. IgG4-related disease is well documented to involve extraocular muscles, commonly producing a restrictive pattern.4IgG4-related disease can affect both the muscle belly and its tendinous attachment, whereas thyroid orbitopathy typically spares the tendon.2Notably, the lateral rectus is disproportionately involved in patients with singular or multiple muscle involvement.2Biopsy of the affected lateral rectus muscle revealed a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease, ruling out other such considerations as metastatic disease, giant cell myositis, sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and amyloidosis (Figure 2). IgG4-related disease is an insidious, progressive, multisystem fibroinflammatory disease that can affect hepatobiliary ducts, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes, salivary glands, retroperitoneum, pancreas, and lymph nodes, among other areas.5Its prevalence is estimated at 0.28 to 1.08 per 100 000 individuals,5with a mean age at diagnosis in the late 50s.6Although IgG4-related disease is slightly more prevalent in men (1:0.64-0.77), IgG4-related orbital disease (IgG4-ROD) affects men and women equally.6IgG4-ROD most commonly affects the lacrimal gland but can also affect extraocular muscles, orbit, adnexal soft tissue, and the cavernous sinus.6Other neurological involvement includes hypertrophic pachymeningitis, hypophysitis, peripheral neuropathy, and parenchymal disease.6 Although not well understood, the pathogenesis of IgG4-related disease involves complex immunogenic interactions between B cells and CD4+T lymphocytes within the affected organ, leading to release of local cytokines that produce an irregular, whorled pattern of fibrosis (“storiform fibrosis”) at the site of disease.5,6Within a germinal center of a lymph node or other lymphoid tissue, B cells also undergo preferential production of IgG4, and T helper cells facilitate class switching to IgG4.5,6In a healthy adult, IgG4 comprises less than 5% of the body’s immunoglobulins.7Elevated IgG4 levels above 135 mg/L support a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease, but this may be normal in 30% of patients.7 Most patients with IgG4-ROD present with bilateral eyelid swelling and proptosis; however, diplopia is the presenting feature in one-third of patients.6IgG4-ROD results in a lesser degree of restrictive strabismus and diplopia than thyroid orbitopathy, despite having greater extraocular enlargement.4MRI may demonstrate a well-defined tumorlike mass within the structures of the orbit and/or abnormal thickening of extraocular muscles. The regions of abnormality are isointense on T1, have variable patterns of T2 signal change, and homogenously enhance on postgadolinium images.8Enlargement of the infraorbital nerve on MRI is a specific sign for IgG4-ROD but lacks sensitivity.9Involvement of the infraorbital nerve is minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic, as infiltration is typically limited to the epineurium.4In the absence of reliable serological and radiographical markers, the diagnosis of IgG4-ROD hinges on histopathological confirmation of lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with an increased ratio of IgG4-positive to IgG-positive plasmacytes equal to or greater than 40%, or more than 50 IgG4-positive cells per high-power field.10The classic findings of storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis in IgG4-related disease are less frequently seen in IgG4-ROD compared with other sites of disease.10 Early recognition and treatment can prevent long-term complications and death in patients with IgG4-related disease. On confirmation of IgG4-ROD, treatment with high-dose corticosteroids and rituximab should be initiated. Although systemic IgG4-related disease may be treated with corticosteroid monotherapy, combination therapy of corticosteroids and rituximab is preferred in patients with severe disease, neurological involvement, and high IgG4 levels.6

case_info.explanation: This case illustrates the diagnostic considerations of a patient with enlarged extraocular muscles. Although this most commonly occurs in thyroid eye disease, the patient was euthyroid and did not have the typical restrictive pattern of ocular dysmotility, whereby duction in the opposite direction of the enlarged muscle is impaired.1Thyroid orbitopathy classically affects a combination of the inferior rectus, medial rectus, and/or levator palpebrae superioris.2Isolated involvement of the lateral rectus, superior rectus, or oblique muscles is virtually absent in thyroid disease.2Ocular lymphoma involving the extraocular muscles is rare, with 1 review identifying 46 cases in the literature3; it more commonly affects the lacrimal glands or the intraconal or extraconal orbital compartment. Ocular lymphoma can cause weakness of the enlarged extraocular muscles, whereas metastatic deposits result in a restrictive pattern.1Features of malignancy include the presence of a focal mass, irregular edges, or nodularity within the muscle.2Although single muscle involvement is often seen in idiopathic inflammatory orbital myositis, the lack of pain argues against the diagnosis. IgG4-related disease is well documented to involve extraocular muscles, commonly producing a restrictive pattern.4IgG4-related disease can affect both the muscle belly and its tendinous attachment, whereas thyroid orbitopathy typically spares the tendon.2Notably, the lateral rectus is disproportionately involved in patients with singular or multiple muscle involvement.2Biopsy of the affected lateral rectus muscle revealed a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease, ruling out other such considerations as metastatic disease, giant cell myositis, sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and amyloidosis (Figure 2). IgG4-related disease is an insidious, progressive, multisystem fibroinflammatory disease that can affect hepatobiliary ducts, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes, salivary glands, retroperitoneum, pancreas, and lymph nodes, among other areas.5Its prevalence is estimated at 0.28 to 1.08 per 100 000 individuals,5with a mean age at diagnosis in the late 50s.6Although IgG4-related disease is slightly more prevalent in men (1:0.64-0.77), IgG4-related orbital disease (IgG4-ROD) affects men and women equally.6IgG4-ROD most commonly affects the lacrimal gland but can also affect extraocular muscles, orbit, adnexal soft tissue, and the cavernous sinus.6Other neurological involvement includes hypertrophic pachymeningitis, hypophysitis, peripheral neuropathy, and parenchymal disease.6 Although not well understood, the pathogenesis of IgG4-related disease involves complex immunogenic interactions between B cells and CD4+T lymphocytes within the affected organ, leading to release of local cytokines that produce an irregular, whorled pattern of fibrosis (“storiform fibrosis”) at the site of disease.5,6Within a germinal center of a lymph node or other lymphoid tissue, B cells also undergo preferential production of IgG4, and T helper cells facilitate class switching to IgG4.5,6In a healthy adult, IgG4 comprises less than 5% of the body’s immunoglobulins.7Elevated IgG4 levels above 135 mg/L support a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease, but this may be normal in 30% of patients.7 Most patients with IgG4-ROD present with bilateral eyelid swelling and proptosis; however, diplopia is the presenting feature in one-third of patients.6IgG4-ROD results in a lesser degree of restrictive strabismus and diplopia than thyroid orbitopathy, despite having greater extraocular enlargement.4MRI may demonstrate a well-defined tumorlike mass within the structures of the orbit and/or abnormal thickening of extraocular muscles. The regions of abnormality are isointense on T1, have variable patterns of T2 signal change, and homogenously enhance on postgadolinium images.8Enlargement of the infraorbital nerve on MRI is a specific sign for IgG4-ROD but lacks sensitivity.9Involvement of the infraorbital nerve is minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic, as infiltration is typically limited to the epineurium.4In the absence of reliable serological and radiographical markers, the diagnosis of IgG4-ROD hinges on histopathological confirmation of lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with an increased ratio of IgG4-positive to IgG-positive plasmacytes equal to or greater than 40%, or more than 50 IgG4-positive cells per high-power field.10The classic findings of storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis in IgG4-related disease are less frequently seen in IgG4-ROD compared with other sites of disease.10 Early recognition and treatment can prevent long-term complications and death in patients with IgG4-related disease. On confirmation of IgG4-ROD, treatment with high-dose corticosteroids and rituximab should be initiated. Although systemic IgG4-related disease may be treated with corticosteroid monotherapy, combination therapy of corticosteroids and rituximab is preferred in patients with severe disease, neurological involvement, and high IgG4 levels.6

case_info.explanation: This case illustrates the diagnostic considerations of a patient with enlarged extraocular muscles. Although this most commonly occurs in thyroid eye disease, the patient was euthyroid and did not have the typical restrictive pattern of ocular dysmotility, whereby duction in the opposite direction of the enlarged muscle is impaired.1Thyroid orbitopathy classically affects a combination of the inferior rectus, medial rectus, and/or levator palpebrae superioris.2Isolated involvement of the lateral rectus, superior rectus, or oblique muscles is virtually absent in thyroid disease.2Ocular lymphoma involving the extraocular muscles is rare, with 1 review identifying 46 cases in the literature3; it more commonly affects the lacrimal glands or the intraconal or extraconal orbital compartment. Ocular lymphoma can cause weakness of the enlarged extraocular muscles, whereas metastatic deposits result in a restrictive pattern.1Features of malignancy include the presence of a focal mass, irregular edges, or nodularity within the muscle.2Although single muscle involvement is often seen in idiopathic inflammatory orbital myositis, the lack of pain argues against the diagnosis. IgG4-related disease is well documented to involve extraocular muscles, commonly producing a restrictive pattern.4IgG4-related disease can affect both the muscle belly and its tendinous attachment, whereas thyroid orbitopathy typically spares the tendon.2Notably, the lateral rectus is disproportionately involved in patients with singular or multiple muscle involvement.2Biopsy of the affected lateral rectus muscle revealed a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease, ruling out other such considerations as metastatic disease, giant cell myositis, sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and amyloidosis (Figure 2). IgG4-related disease is an insidious, progressive, multisystem fibroinflammatory disease that can affect hepatobiliary ducts, kidneys, lungs, lymph nodes, salivary glands, retroperitoneum, pancreas, and lymph nodes, among other areas.5Its prevalence is estimated at 0.28 to 1.08 per 100 000 individuals,5with a mean age at diagnosis in the late 50s.6Although IgG4-related disease is slightly more prevalent in men (1:0.64-0.77), IgG4-related orbital disease (IgG4-ROD) affects men and women equally.6IgG4-ROD most commonly affects the lacrimal gland but can also affect extraocular muscles, orbit, adnexal soft tissue, and the cavernous sinus.6Other neurological involvement includes hypertrophic pachymeningitis, hypophysitis, peripheral neuropathy, and parenchymal disease.6 Although not well understood, the pathogenesis of IgG4-related disease involves complex immunogenic interactions between B cells and CD4+T lymphocytes within the affected organ, leading to release of local cytokines that produce an irregular, whorled pattern of fibrosis (“storiform fibrosis”) at the site of disease.5,6Within a germinal center of a lymph node or other lymphoid tissue, B cells also undergo preferential production of IgG4, and T helper cells facilitate class switching to IgG4.5,6In a healthy adult, IgG4 comprises less than 5% of the body’s immunoglobulins.7Elevated IgG4 levels above 135 mg/L support a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease, but this may be normal in 30% of patients.7 Most patients with IgG4-ROD present with bilateral eyelid swelling and proptosis; however, diplopia is the presenting feature in one-third of patients.6IgG4-ROD results in a lesser degree of restrictive strabismus and diplopia than thyroid orbitopathy, despite having greater extraocular enlargement.4MRI may demonstrate a well-defined tumorlike mass within the structures of the orbit and/or abnormal thickening of extraocular muscles. The regions of abnormality are isointense on T1, have variable patterns of T2 signal change, and homogenously enhance on postgadolinium images.8Enlargement of the infraorbital nerve on MRI is a specific sign for IgG4-ROD but lacks sensitivity.9Involvement of the infraorbital nerve is minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic, as infiltration is typically limited to the epineurium.4In the absence of reliable serological and radiographical markers, the diagnosis of IgG4-ROD hinges on histopathological confirmation of lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with an increased ratio of IgG4-positive to IgG-positive plasmacytes equal to or greater than 40%, or more than 50 IgG4-positive cells per high-power field.10The classic findings of storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis in IgG4-related disease are less frequently seen in IgG4-ROD compared with other sites of disease.10 Early recognition and treatment can prevent long-term complications and death in patients with IgG4-related disease. On confirmation of IgG4-ROD, treatment with high-dose corticosteroids and rituximab should be initiated. Although systemic IgG4-related disease may be treated with corticosteroid monotherapy, combination therapy of corticosteroids and rituximab is preferred in patients with severe disease, neurological involvement, and high IgG4 levels.6
